lesson.title: The One Frequency That Defines the Whole Wave
lesson.summary: The fundamental frequency is the repetition rate of a periodic signal, the reciprocal of its period, and it serves as the base note against which every other frequency component in that signal is measured.
lesson.body:
For any periodic signal with period T, the fundamental frequency is defined as f0 = 1/T. In words, it is simply how many times per second the signal's pattern repeats, which is the same frequency concept from earlier chapters (cycles per second, measured in hertz) applied specifically to a periodic signal's repetition rate.

A quick worked example shows the relationship clearly. Suppose a digital circuit's clock signal is a square wave with period T = 1 ms = 0.001 s. Its fundamental frequency is f0 = 1 / 0.001 s = 1000 Hz, or 1 kHz. Now suppose the period were cut in half, to T = 0.5 ms. The fundamental frequency becomes f0 = 1 / 0.0005 s = 2000 Hz, or 2 kHz, exactly double. Halving the period doubles the fundamental frequency, which is just the inverse relationship between period and frequency playing out with real numbers.

The word "fundamental" is doing real work here, not just decoration. As the next chapter on harmonics shows, a periodic signal that is not itself a pure sine wave, like that clock's square wave, is not actually a single pure tone at f0. It is a mixture of many sinusoidal components layered on top of each other. The fundamental frequency is the lowest of those component frequencies, and it is also the one that matches the signal's overall, visible repetition rate: the period you would measure with an oscilloscope corresponds to 1/f0, not to any of the higher frequency components hiding inside the waveform. Every other frequency present in the signal sits at a whole-number multiple of f0. A useful musical analogy: f0 is the note you perceive as the pitch, while the higher components, the harmonics, add the overtones that give an instrument its distinctive timbre without changing which note you hear.
